title: Harnessing Streaming Video in the Wild
claim: A multi-part streaming system and benchmark jointly cover capabilities that prior baselines and offline benchmarks each leave uncovered.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; radar chart, system diagram, comparison table, timelines
description: A four-quadrant composite figure. Top-left is a triangular radar chart with axes for long-horizon memory, proactive interaction and real-time inference. Four baselines (Closed-Source MLLMs, StreamingVLM, StreamForest, LiveStar) show as small shapes, and a large pink StreamingHarness triangle covers nearly the whole area. Bottom-left is a pink and blue pipeline diagram. User query and video frames feed a VLM and the central Streaming Harness block. Beside it are a short, mid and long-term memory stack with compression arrows, plus sub-second latency, response/silence and in-the-wild dataset training boxes. Top-right is a benchmark-by-capability table of red ✗ and green ✓ marks, where only Streaming-Eval has every check. Below it are two filmstrip panels. A grey single-turn offline strip has one question and one answer. A multi-turn live strip has colored Q&A bubbles along egocentric video frames.
caption: Top-left: StreamingHarness jointly delivers proactive interaction, long-horizon memory, and real-time inference—capabilities that no prior baseline satisfies simultaneously. Bottom-left: Overview of the StreamingHarness. Top-right: Comparative overview of Streaming-Eval and existing benchmarks. Bottom-right: Unlike single-turn offline benchmarks, Streaming-Eval assesses six in-the-wild capabilities (Proactive, Punctual, Contextual, Forward, Present, Backward).
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly required to process unbounded video streams in applications such as video-call assistants, live commentary, and embodied robots. An ideal streaming system should support proactive interaction, long-horizon memory, and real-time processing, while resting on a VLM backbone capable of handling diverse in-the-wild streaming tasks. However, existing VLMs excel at offline video understanding but fall short in streaming capabilities and lack dedicated infrastructure for streaming deployment. We address this gap on three fronts. (i) For backbone capability, we construct \textbf{Streaming-Train-248K}, a streaming dataset paired with a novel training objective for adapting VLMs to streaming interaction and understanding. (ii) For real-world deployment, we introduce \textbf{Streaming Harness}, a plug-and-play system that endows any VLM with three core abilities: proactive interaction (per-second response decisions), long-term memory (12-hour context retention), and real-time processing (sub-second latency). (iii) To drive continued community progress on streaming capabilities, we design \textbf{Streaming-Eval}, a benchmark that reflects models' capabilities across diverse in-the-wild scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent gains from our approach across all core capabilities required for streaming video understanding. We will open-source our data, code, and benchmark to advance the community's shift from offline video understanding to deployable streaming intelligence.
